problem: LiDAR/occupancy-based navigation policies such as MPC cannot perceive nuanced human non-verbal cues like gestures, so they cannot produce socially compliant behavior in response to them. End-to-end pixel-to-control learning needs large datasets and overfits to robot dynamics.
motivation: Humans use gestures to negotiate passage in dense spaces, so social robots must interpret them. RGB captures gestures, while LiDAR-based MPC gives safe low-level control, so combining the two lets each cover the other's weakness.
key_idea: A 3D-conv sequential network trained by imitation on RGB and occupancy-map sequences predicts future waypoint deltas from gestures, and these are fed as intermediate goals to an iLQR MPC controller.
insight: Splitting the problem into a high-level gesture-aware waypoint predictor and a low-level MPC keeps collision-free control while adding gesture responsiveness. The user study shows the gain comes almost entirely from Q3 (Correctness), the only question with a significant ANOVA effect. Safety was rated higher for baseline MPC, which gives humans more room, and Gesture2Path took longer to reach the goal. There is no ablation of the architecture.
method: Sequential network: 3D-conv layers embed 10-step subsequences of 256x256 RGB images and occupancy maps into two 64-d embeddings. The goal delta is projected to 64-d, the embeddings are added, and three dense layers with linear output regress l=10 position deltas.

Imitation learning: trained with an L2 loss and Adam on 277 teleoperated real-world trajectories, split 90/10 into train/validation. The checkpoint with the lowest validation L2 is used; training takes about 6 hours on a V100.
Waypoint generation: the intermediate target p_t = p_n + sum of the predicted deltas. The network re-plans every k=10 steps, so it can react to changes in the gesture.

Low-level MPC: the Trajax iLQR solver takes the occupancy grid and relative goal and outputs linear and angular velocities at 10 Hz. The cost combines goal, collision-margin and control penalties. MPC may deviate from the predicted path for safety.

Gesture scenarios and protocol: four gestures (left, right, follow me, make a circle) with three trained policies (Circle, Follow, Left/Right). Evaluation uses an in-situ Likert questionnaire (Safe, Clarity, Correct, Trust) following a social-navigation protocol.

setting.backbone: 3D-CNN sequential network (trained from scratch) + iLQR MPC (Trajax, hand-engineered cost)
setting.training_data: 277 real-world teleoperated demonstration trajectories (40 follow, 30 circle, 207 left/right), 20-40 s each
setting.observation: head-mounted RGB camera sequences + 2D LiDAR occupancy grid + robot position on a static map
setting.action_space: linear and angular velocity commands from MPC, tracking predicted intermediate waypoints
setting.privileged: static map of the environment for localization; known goal position

numbers_note: No standard navigation benchmark. Results are user-study Likert ratings shown only in figures, plus a table of average durations (Gesture2Path vs MPC, sec: Circle 56/35, Follow 45/38, Left 45/38, Right 46/33) and p-values.
results: In a within-subjects study with 12 participants, Gesture2Path was rated higher than the MPC baseline for all four gestures (paired t-test p<.01). The difference is driven by correctness (Q3); ANOVA on Q1, Q2 and Q4 was not significant. MPC was rated safer and faster, while Gesture2Path took longer paths, and Left/Right performed worse than Circle/Follow.
limitations: Small user study (12 participants, mostly robot-experienced) with few trials; the Left/Right MPC baseline had only 5 trials and gesture performance varies across people.
One separate policy is trained per gesture set, and the policies handle only a single human; multi-gesture and multi-human handling is future work.
Lower safety ratings and longer durations than MPC; the network and MPC are loosely coupled; no ablations or quantitative benchmark.
builds_on: Social navigation evaluation protocol (Pirk et al. 2022)
compares_to: Reinforcement-learning long-range navigation policy (Francis et al. 2020)
